# How can I get text to speech translations in offline mode?

I've downloaded the languages (french and arabic) to use them without needing internet, but I can only use the text to speech option with spanish (native language), so I was wondering if there is any option to download voice packages or something or that's managed by the phone.

Offline Speech output has never been supported directly by the Google Translate app. The Translate app itself does not download the data for Text To Speech (TTS) output.

I say "directly" because depending on your phone -- the text to speech system on your phone \*may\* work offline, depending on if it is Samsung TTS, Google/Pixel TTS, Motorola TTS, etc. When online, the Translate app requests TTS audio from Google servers. When offline, we fall back to the TTS as available on your particular phone, and whether the Android OS (not Google's) TTS service reports it can speak for a given language when offline. Depending on your phone's TTS setup (Samsung, Pixel, OnePlus, etc) -- TTS may work offline if your phone is so configured.

There is no ability for the Translate app to communicate or coordinate with each phone's TTS -- so offline TTS is hit-or-miss at this point. If you are able to download TTS offline in your phone's settings, then this may work, but Translate is unable to link you there or perform this configuration for you.

It's possible to include Google TTS with Translate, but the team is not in a position to develop such a feature at this time.

# Download languages to use offline

Android phone & tabletiPhone & iPad

More

More

You can download languages onto your device. This lets you translate them without an internet connection.

After you’ve downloaded a language, you could be able to translate it by looking at it through your device's camera lens. [See languages that work with instant camera translations](https://support.google.com/translate/answer/6142483).

## Choose & download languages

1. Before you download languages, connect to Wi-Fi.
2. Open the Translate app ![Translate app](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/zbjy4lVco3DJT8GqHw3TXq74-q7utDszuEWMeKIpDcQTG-jL5v82cUTBy1wg=w16).
3. At the bottom, select the language you want to download.
4. Next to the language, tap Download ![](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/Xv_MeSheQLE6J9BLMqGbHnTNNxLUmILa3K4D2gfLbmyySjXzW3smBzecUdy6EP00I7w=w18).

   - If it’s not there, the language can’t be downloaded.
   - If it asks you to download the language file, tap **Download**.

**Tip:** In the Translate app, your saved languages show up as Downloaded ![](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/jpqh5kz_17k9ppEdam4C_65OOirxvrnMJ7vlqt36sw8O6VaiXcW6f6_f5DN9Yw=w18).

### Download languages without Wi-Fi

Since language files are small, when you’re not connected to Wi-Fi, you can download them with mobile data. If you don’t use Wi-Fi, it may affect your mobile carrier charges.

1. On your Android phone or tablet, open the Translate app ![Translate app](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/zbjy4lVco3DJT8GqHw3TXq74-q7utDszuEWMeKIpDcQTG-jL5v82cUTBy1wg=w16).
2. Tap Menu ![](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/UYVGdnOY33gkFyAvmY4Xa1Se8-bLinBEnU35eQ3kMlBrgHWj9g3AU6O-ekxOdxqkERk=w36-h36)![and then](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/QbWcYKta5vh_4-OgUeFmK-JOB0YgLLoGh69P478nE6mKdfpWQniiBabjF7FVoCVXI0g=h36) Settings ![Settings](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/357M8Fx_lLhnrWQd9imNXnB9lDqgu0a0t-9d6xzF1aU82S4S-3FBi86iLFjvieQkbV4Z=w36-h36)![and then](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/QbWcYKta5vh_4-OgUeFmK-JOB0YgLLoGh69P478nE6mKdfpWQniiBabjF7FVoCVXI0g=h36)**Data usage**.
3. Tap **Downloaded languages**.

   - **To always confirm before you download without Wi-Fi:** Tap **Ask before downloading**.
   - **To always use mobile data when you can't use Wi-Fi:** Tap **Use Wi-Fi or mobile network**.

## Update or remove languages

1. Connect to Wi-Fi.
2. On your Android phone or tablet, open the Translate app ![Translate app](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/zbjy4lVco3DJT8GqHw3TXq74-q7utDszuEWMeKIpDcQTG-jL5v82cUTBy1wg=w16).

4. You’ll get a list of available languages.
   - **To upgrade a language to a higher-quality language pack:** Next to the language, tap **Upgrade**.
   - **To update a language on your device:** Next to the language, tap **Update**.
   - **To delete a language from your device:** Tap Remove ![](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/omPP8k3T58rWn37iYHeqxPBOgiN6-8ILrPob4vuEdXX62w2a6efMb6114n-qQa06570=w36-h36). When asked if you want to remove the downloaded package, tap **Remove**.

Code embedded in the latest Google Translate Android update suggests that Google is building offline support for Live Translate, its real-time spoken conversation feature. Right now, attempting to use Google Translate's live translation feature offline throws an error. But that may be about to change, [as per reports](https://www.androidauthority.com/google-translate-live-offline-3666725/).

The signals appear in the app version `10.17.48.914427315.6-release` for Android. Google has not confirmed a release date or made any official announcement. This is teardown reporting based on in-app signals, not a product launch.

## What the teardown found

The offline mechanism appears to mirror how text-based offline translation already works in Google Translate. Users would need to pre-download the relevant language pack before losing connectivity; after that, no active internet connection would be required during the conversation itself, according to Android Authority.

Based on in-app UI indicators observed in the update, the initial offline language set appears to include English, French, German, Portuguese, Italian, and Spanish. Google also appears to be building explicit in-app labels to identify which languages will support Live offline. That design choice could indicate limited coverage is intentional rather than a placeholder, though the teardown evidence doesn't settle it definitively.

The six languages would be a narrow slice of the 70-plus languages available in the online mode. When Google launched the Gemini-powered live conversation feature in late 2025, it initially [rolled out to users in the U.S., India, and Mexico](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/translate/language-learning-live-translate/) before expanding further. All six likely offline candidates are major European languages with large existing user bases, which is consistent with how phased rollouts have worked before, though that pattern doesn't confirm what Google is planning here.

Google has not confirmed which devices will support offline Live Translate, what the full language list will be at launch, or when the feature will ship.

## Why Google Translate offline live translation is harder to build than text

The existing downloadable language packs only handle text and image translation, reports confirmed. Spoken conversation is a different category of problem.

Text translation offline is relatively contained. A compressed language model takes typed input, processes it, and returns output without any audio pipeline involved. Real-time speech translation is three sequential operations running on the device itself: recognizing spoken audio in one language, translating it, then synthesizing audible output in another, with very low latency, with no server available to share the computational load. That's why spoken conversation has stayed online-only even as offline text support has existed in the app for years. The device has to do everything, fast, on battery power.

Google has been working on this problem at the research level. In June 2024, researchers from Google Research and Google DeepMind presented SimulTron, described in their paper as "the first method to demonstrate real-time S2ST on a device." It ran on consumer mobile hardware and outperformed prior real-time approaches on both translation accuracy and latency, [according to a Slator summary of the research](https://slator.com/google-presents-first-on-device-real-time-speech-to-speech-translation-model/). The researchers framed on-device speech-to-speech translation as essential, given how central smartphones have become to personal and professional communication.

That research doesn't confirm the Translate app feature uses SimulTron's specific architecture. It does show Google has spent serious engineering effort on the underlying problem and that the hardware constraints are surmountable on consumer devices. More than a year of development since that paper is also a relevant context.

On-device translation has a longer history on Pixel hardware than many users realize. Google's Pixel support documentation notes that Live Translate for text messages runs entirely on the device, with [all translations taking place locally](https://support.google.com/pixelphone/answer/11209263?hl=en). Spoken conversation has been the missing piece of that on-device story. What the current teardown suggests is Google may now be attempting to close it.

## What would change for users

The clearest beneficiaries would be travelers in genuinely low-connectivity situations: underground transit, remote regions, international roaming where data costs are punishing, or an airplane with no Wi-Fi. The workflow would be straightforward in principle: download the relevant language pack on a Wi-Fi connection before departing, then use Live Translate anywhere without touching mobile data.

There's a privacy dimension worth noting. If Google processes offline conversations entirely on-device, spoken audio may not need to be sent to Google's servers during the session. That would be a meaningful structural difference from the current cloud-based mode. Google has not confirmed how the offline mode will handle audio processing, however, and the teardown evidence doesn't answer that question.

The current online Live Translate uses Gemini's multimodal capabilities to identify conversational pauses, accents, and intonations, according to Google. An on-device model running on phone hardware operates under tighter constraints, and an offline model is necessarily smaller and more specialized than its cloud counterpart. Language coverage will be narrower. Accuracy and naturalness may differ from the cloud version, particularly for fast speech, regional accents, or speakers who switch between languages mid-sentence. None of that is confirmed in the teardown, but it's a reasonable baseline expectation for any offline-first AI feature.

## What remains unconfirmed

Several specifics are still entirely open. Google has not said anything publicly about storage requirements for offline speech packs, battery impact during extended sessions, which device models will support the feature, or whether the offline mode will deliver full speech-to-speech audio output or fall back to transcription-based translation. The gap between those two would matter considerably in a real conversation.

Whether iOS will receive offline Live Translate is also unresolved. Google launched the original online feature on both Android and iOS nine months ago, per the Google Blog, but all current evidence for the offline version is Android-specific. That could mean a staggered launch is planned, or it could simply reflect the nature of teardown reporting, which surfaces what's in a given app build and nothing more.

## A parallel development worth watching

The offline capability isn't the only limitation Google appears to be addressing. Months ago, [Android Authority reported](https://www.androidauthority.com/google-translate-preps-xr-changes-3616845/) that Google was working on background persistence for Live Translate, a persistent notification system that would allow the feature to keep translating speech even when users switch to another app. Currently, Live Translate stops the moment you leave the Google Translate app. The proposed fix would work similarly to how Gemini Live maintains a notification when you multitask.

That's a separate limitation from the offline gap, but the two are connected in practice. A traveler navigating an unfamiliar city needs to be able to glance at a map app or check a booking confirmation without losing their translation session. Offline access handles the connectivity problem; background persistence handles the usability problem. Both need to be solved for Live Translate to work reliably in the situations where it would be most valuable.

Whether both improvements ship in the same update or on separate timelines isn't clear from the available evidence. The code suggests Google is working toward both. Everything else — timing, device support, the full language list, and what the feature actually sounds like in practice — is still waiting on Google to say something publicly.

Seeing “I'm sorry, the translation of this text is temporarily unavailable.” usually means the translation request failed, not that the original text has disappeared or become invalid. The cause may be a brief service interruption, an unstable connection, unsupported content, incorrect language detection, or a problem within one app feature. The checks below help you determine whether to retry, change a setting, clean up the source text, or switch tools.

## **What Does Translation Temporarily Unavailable Mean?**

The wording is broad because the translation layer often cannot identify the exact failure for the user.

### **The Translation Request Failed, Not Necessarily the Original Content**

Translation is usually a separate process applied after an app, browser, or website loads the source. A failure can occur when the platform sends the text to a translation service, detects its language, or receives the result. If you can still read, select, or copy the original, the content itself probably remains available.

### **The Problem May Be Temporary or Limited to One Translation Feature**

One failed caption does not prove that Google Translate is not working everywhere. Camera translation, webpage translation, typed text, speech, and an in-app “Translate” button may use different permissions, language support, or processing paths. Test another item and another mode before reinstalling anything.

### **Common Causes Include Connection, Language, Content, or Service Issues**

Weak connectivity, VPN or firewall filtering, an unsupported language pair, and incorrect automatic detection are frequent causes. Translation may also fail on extremely long text, mixed scripts, decorative characters, images without recognized text, or content loaded dynamically. Less often, the provider or the platform hosting the content is experiencing an outage.![iFLYTEK translator as offline fallback](https://img-va.myshopline.com/image/store/1712541173749/iflytek-smart-translator-4.webp?w=836&h=556)

## **Where Does This Translation Error Appear and How Can You Check It?**

The location of the error is the fastest clue because it shows which part of the workflow to test.

### **Identify Where the Translation Error Appears**

Note whether the failure affects a social post, an entire webpage, a message, an image, or a dedicated translation app. Also record whether the original content loads and whether the problem affects one item or everything. That distinction separates a content-specific problem from an account, device, network, or service issue.

### **Run a Quick Test to Narrow Down the Cause**

Use a short, plain sentence in a language you can identify, then repeat the request on another item or translation mode. The comparison is more useful than repeatedly tapping the same button.

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Where the Problem Appears** | **Typical Symptom** | **Quick Check** | **What the Result Suggests** |
| Social media posts, captions, or comments | One item fails while others work | Reload it and translate another item | A source-language, formatting, or content restriction is likely |
| Webpages and browser translation | The page or some sections remain untranslated | Refresh, test another site, and try copying the affected text | Scripts, frames, dynamic content, or page formatting may be blocking translation |
| Messaging apps and mobile keyboards | Message or typing translation stops | Try a simple sentence elsewhere and select both languages manually | The original message, conversation, or app is probably responsible |
| Images, videos, or scans | Visible words are not detected | Check clarity, cropping, orientation, and text recognition | Image quality, OCR, or unsupported visual content is the likely cause |
| Standalone translation apps | Text, voice, camera, or offline mode fails | Test a short typed sentence in each mode | One feature may be failing rather than the whole app |
| Several apps or websites | Multiple tools fail together | Switch between Wi-Fi and mobile data | A VPN, proxy, firewall, or local network setting may be interfering |

## **How to Fix Translation Temporarily Unavailable Step by Step**

Start with reversible checks and stop as soon as translation works; resetting the app first can erase useful settings or downloaded languages.

### **Step 1: Retry the Translation and Reload the Original Content**

Wait briefly, retry once, and then refresh the post, page, or conversation. Reopen the app if necessary. This clears stale page state and temporary request failures without changing your data; repeated rapid retries rarely help during a service-side problem.

### **Step 2: Check the Connection and Remove Network Restrictions**

Open another live webpage, then switch from Wi-Fi to mobile data or the reverse. Temporarily disable a VPN, proxy, private DNS filter, or strict firewall only if your security policy permits it. If translation works on the alternate network, troubleshoot the original network instead of the translation app.

### **Step 3: Manually Set the Source and Target Languages**

Replace automatic language detection with the actual source language and confirm the target language. Short phrases, names, mixed-language messages, and closely related languages can be misidentified. A full sentence provides more context than an isolated word, a practice also reflected in [**Google's instructions for written translation**](https://support.google.com/translate/answer/6142478) **.**

### **Step 4: Clean the Text and Isolate the Problem Section**

Copy the text into a plain-text field and remove excessive emoji, invisible formatting, repeated punctuation, or broken line spacing. Divide a long passage into smaller meaningful sections rather than individual words. If one segment consistently fails, inspect it for unusual symbols, mixed scripts, confidential-content controls, or unsupported material.

### **Step 5: Update and Reset the Affected Translation Feature**

Update the app and operating system, restart the browser or device, and ensure JavaScript and required permissions are enabled. Next, clear the browser cache for the affected site or the app cache where the operating system permits. Reinstall only after saving phrasebooks or other local data and noting which offline language packs must be downloaded again.

### **Step 6: Check Account, Region, and Language Availability**

Sign out and test again only when the feature normally works without an account; otherwise, verify account age, administrator controls, and regional availability. Not every language supports every mode, and website translation is not available in all regions according to [**Google Translate Help**](https://support.google.com/translate/answer/2534559) **.** A disabled speech or download button may indicate unsupported availability rather than a fault.

### **Step 7: Check for a Service Outage or Test Another Device**

Test the same short sentence on a second device or through the provider's web interface. If it fails across devices and networks, look for an official status page or support notice and wait before changing more settings. If only one device fails, compare app versions, permissions, storage, date and time settings, and network configuration.![Translation temporarily unavailable on phone](https://img-va.myshopline.com/image/store/1712541173749/unnamed-6-1.webp?w=800&h=530)

## **What to Use When Built-In Translation Still Does Not Work**

Choose a fallback based on the source format, privacy requirements, connectivity, and how often the problem occurs.

### **Paste the Original Text Into a Separate Translation Tool**

Copyable text is quickest to test in a standalone translator. Paste one complete section, set both languages manually, and compare the result with context you understand. Avoid uploading confidential contracts, health records, internal messages, or personal data unless the tool's privacy terms and your organization's policy permit it.

### **Use Screenshot or Photo Translation for Visual Content**

For subtitles, scanned notices, menus, or text embedded in an image, capture a sharp, tightly cropped image with good contrast. Straighten the image and remove unrelated text so optical character recognition can identify the correct reading order. If accuracy matters, verify names, numbers, dates, warnings, and technical terms against the original.

### **Use a Translation App With Downloaded Offline Languages**

When traveling with poor reception or limited mobile data, you may wonder, does Google Translate work offline? It does, as long as you download the required language packs before leaving a reliable network. Google states that downloaded languages can be used for translation without an internet connection, although languages without a download option are not available offline, and downloaded packs may occasionally require updates ( **[Android](https://support.google.com/translate/answer/6142473)**, **[iPhone and iPad](https://support.google.com/translate/answer/6142473)**). Offline translation can be useful for everyday phrases while traveling, though language availability and translation results may differ from online modes.

Real-time voice translation once required massive cloud servers. Today, your Android can translate spoken conversations completely off the grid—if you download the right files first.

The phone instantly transcribes and translates the conversation via voice without ever sending a byte of data to the cloud.

If you do not have a compatible Samsung device, Google Translate is your best option on Android, though it requires a bit of specific configuration to work entirely offline.

To set up Google Translate for off-grid voice translation:

- Open the app, tap your profile icon, and select Downloaded languages. Download both your native language and the language you need.
- Ensure your phone's built-in speech recognition is also configured for offline use. On most Android devices, this means going into your system settings and downloading the offline speech-to-text pack for those same languages (often managed by Google Voice Typing or Gboard).

Once configured, Google Translate will allow you to speak into the app, convert your voice to text, translate it, and read it aloud using offline text-to-speech. The offline voice translation might be slightly less nuanced than the online version—which uses cloud processing for better context—but it is highly reliable for travel phrases.

It is crucial to test your setup before you travel. Put your phone in Airplane Mode, turn off Wi-Fi, and try having a mock conversation.
